looks.look: The Joint Program Office photograph shows a seated pilot wearing an olive-green flight suit, a dark helmet with a large reflective visor, and an oxygen mask connected to a corrugated hose. A tall, dark ejection-seat headrest rises behind the helmet. This documents equipment, not either fictional character’s identity, age, ethnicity or facial appearance. ([jsf.mil](https://www.jsf.mil/themes/f35/images/050.jpg))

looks.thing: F-35 helmet-mounted display and oxygen mask
looks.look: Figure 7, printed page 37, shows a rounded, dark, visibly patterned helmet shell; a broad wraparound reflective visor; a small circular forehead-mounted optical component; and a gray-and-black oxygen mask with a ribbed breathing hose. Use this as a dated equipment reference, not a conventional fighter helmet with separate external night-vision goggles. ([gao.gov](https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-19-341.pdf))

The Joint Program Office specifies a wide, 20-by-8-inch glass-cockpit touchscreen. Its accompanying photograph shows dark cockpit surfaces and the pilot seated beneath the canopy. The F-35 uses helmet-projected information rather than a separate physical head-up display in front of the pilot. ([jsf.mil](https://www.jsf.mil/cockpit))

Lockheed Martin’s identification guide documents two intakes, two tails and one round engine exhaust. The C variant has larger wings than the A/B variants, visible wing-fold hinge lines, a full-length canopy, a right-side refueling probe, and two nosewheel tires with a launch bar. The underside has two distinct main weapon bays, each with two doors. These are useful continuity checks against accidentally using an F-35A, F-35B or F-22 model. ([codeonemagazine.net](https://codeonemagazine.net/c5_article.html?item_id=177))

looks.thing: F-35C paint, markings and bomb-release reference
looks.look: The March 29, 2017 release photograph shows a gray aircraft with contrasting panel outlines, swept wings and outward-canted twin tail fins. This particular test aircraft carries NAVY markings, a U.S. national insignia, ED tail lettering and number 104. Those markings belong to the photographed test aircraft; they should not be presented as generic markings for every operational F-35C. ([media.defense.gov](https://media.defense.gov/2017/Apr/19/2001735224/-1/-1/0/170329-F-ZZ999-463.JPG))

The documented release photograph shows an elongated bomb with a narrow nose-guidance assembly, small forward control surfaces and a larger fin assembly at the rear. The photographed example is an instrumented, explosively inert test weapon, with conspicuous contrasting circular markings along its body; do not copy those markings as evidence of a live operational bomb’s finish. ([media.defense.gov](https://media.defense.gov/2017/Apr/19/2001735224/-1/-1/0/170329-F-ZZ999-463.JPG))

The August 15, 2021 exercise photograph shows a long, low gray warship with a pointed bow, central superstructure, a prominent mast and a low stern, with smoke rising and trailing away. Naval History and Heritage Command identifies Ingraham as an Oliver Hazard Perry-class guided-missile frigate, 453 feet long and 47 feet in beam. The exercise photograph documents its target-hulk appearance; its original armament inventory should not be assumed still present. ([d1ldvf68ux039x.cloudfront.net](https://d1ldvf68ux039x.cloudfront.net/thumbs/photos/2108/6787106/1000w_q95.jpg))

These are the conditions in that image, not a claim that the operating area always looks this way. ([d1ldvf68ux039x.cloudfront.net](https://d1ldvf68ux039x.cloudfront.net/thumbs/photos/2108/6787106/1000w_q95.jpg))

facts.fact: The F-35C is a single-seat, single-engine strike fighter that operates from conventional runways and aircraft carriers. The pilot and wingman therefore occupy separate aircraft, not front and rear seats in one jet.
Keep variant behavior consistent: the F-35C is the catapult-launched carrier variant with folding wingtips. Vertical landing is an F-35B capability, not an F-35C capability.

Radio and visual acknowledgement are real formation practices. Air Force formation-training guidance directs number two to acknowledge a visual signal with a head nod and to use radio to resolve confusion. It also specifies that 'visual' means positive visual contact with a formation aircraft. This supports a restrained acknowledgement beat, but is not evidence of an F-35-specific attack gesture or exact naval combat dialogue.

The F-35 has no separate physical head-up display: flight symbology and sensor imagery are projected onto the helmet visor. Six external infrared cameras provide imagery that can let the pilot see a view otherwise blocked by aircraft structure; the aircraft itself does not become transparent.

An F-35C attack on a ship using laser-guided weapons has a documented precedent. On August 15, 2021, F-35Cs launched from USS Carl Vinson participated in strikes against decommissioned frigate ex-USS Ingraham in the Hawaiian Islands Operating Area. The Navy account does not identify the precise bomb model, and the sinking involved multiple aircraft, ships, missiles and a submarine—not just two F-35s.

The GBU-12 Paveway II is a laser-guided bomb using a 500-pound general-purpose warhead. Laser-guided bombs detect and track a target illuminated by a laser; they should not be portrayed as independently radar-seeking anti-ship missiles.

The F-35C demonstrated GBU-12 employment against a moving land target on March 29, 2017, using an inert bomb and aircraft targeting/release logic. This verifies the aircraft–weapon pairing and a moving-target demonstration; it does not by itself establish performance against a maneuvering, defended warship.

If using the Ingraham exercise as a factual setting, depict a decommissioned target hulk, not an active enemy vessel returning fire. The Navy described environmental preparation and safeguards, with the exercise requiring at least 6,000 feet of water and a location at least 50 nautical miles from land.

story.style: Live-action; steel-gray aircraft against blue ocean, tight cockpit close-ups and sweeping aerial tracking shots in hard golden light.
fact_use: Facts 1–2: Vega and Rook occupy separate F-35Cs, with consistent conventional-flight behavior.
Fact 3: Radio contact and restrained head nods provide the acknowledgement beat.
Fact 4 and cockpit references: Helmet equipment and a wide touchscreen appear without a separate physical head-up display.
Facts 6–7: The F-35Cs release GBU-12 Paveway II laser-guided bombs; the targeting display indicates laser designation.
Documented appearance references inform the flight clothing, aircraft silhouettes and bomb shapes. Meridian Range and Harrow are fictional.
story.story:
Over Meridian Range, Vega’s F-35C and Rook’s F-35C race above blue ocean, gray wings spread, twin tails canted outward. Guitar and drums punch through engine thunder.

Inside Vega’s F-35C, Vega turns a dark helmet toward Rook’s F-35C. Sunlight flashes across the broad reflective visor. A ribbed oxygen hose crosses an olive-green flight suit.

“Rook, you with me?” Vega’s radio crackles.

“Right here, Vega.”

Inside Rook’s F-35C, Rook looks across at Vega and gives one firm nod. Vega nods back.

Ahead, the gray frigate Harrow floats beneath a tall mast. A caption reads: “MERIDIAN RANGE. HARROW: DECOMMISSIONED TARGET.”

On Vega’s wide touchscreen, Harrow sits beneath a crosshair. “LASER” illuminates beside the image.

Vega’s F-35C and Rook’s F-35C bank toward Harrow. Each releases a GBU-12 Paveway II bomb from a wing pylon. The camera follows the two GBU-12 Paveway II bombs downward, narrow noses leading, rear fins spread.

Two impacts punch fire and spray along Harrow. Smoke rolls above the mast.

Vega’s F-35C and Rook’s F-35C climb together. The guitar cuts out.

Black. White lettering: “F-35C. TOGETHER, ON TARGET.”
